extracted.intended_audience: students, journalists, scholars and practitioners interested in public opinion, media, and political communication
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and considerations for how news and information reach publics and shape public opinion, including infrastructural, social, economic, linguistic, and attentional constraints. Useful for analyzing news-homepage design, journalism practice, and studies of mass communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits upon the circulation of ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: While censorship and privacy intercept much information at its source, a very much larger body of fact never reaches the whole public at all, or only very slowly; there are very distinct limits upon the circulation of ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statement frames circulation limits broadly — not only formal censorship but also structural and social limits. Use this as a criterion to evaluate whether and how information actually reaches different segments of the public (speed, reach, and completeness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale and resources required to reach 'everybody'
rubrics_metrics.description: Extreme measures (e.g., wartime propaganda machinery) were required to create something like one public opinion all over America: thousands of releases, tens of thousands of speakers, hundreds of thousands of speeches, distribution via many civic channels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators should note the personnel, money, organizational complexity and multiple channels necessary to achieve rapid, uniform diffusion. In peacetime such scale is typically absent, explaining fragmented publics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infrastructure and transport influence on idea circulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Travel and trade, the mails, the wires, and radio, railroads, highways, ships, motor cars, and aeroplanes are of the utmost influence on the circulation of ideas; each change (new railways, ports, cheaper cables, better highways) affects supply and quality of information and opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how communication and transport infrastructures (and their costs/availability) enable or restrict distribution of news and ideas across regions and groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monopoly, cost, and supply as barriers
rubrics_metrics.description: The monopolizing of cables, of ports, fuel stations, mountain passes, canals, straits, river courses, terminals, market places means a barrier upon the exchange of news and opinion; but cost and available supply are even greater ones — if travel or trading is prohibitive, barriers exist without formal monopoly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider both institutional monopolies and economic barriers (price, scarcity) as constraints on information flows; identify which operates in a given context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Income and community resources determine access
rubrics_metrics.description: The size of a man's income has considerable effect on his access to the world beyond his neighborhood — with money he can travel, buy books and periodicals, and bring within the range of his attention almost any known fact of the world. The income of the individual, and the income of the community determine the amount of communication that is possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use economic status as a predictor of information access (subscriptions, travel, technologies). Evaluate news reach by socioeconomic strata.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-imposed limitations and lack of curiosity
rubrics_metrics.description: Some portions of the sovereign people ... spend most of their spare time and spare money on motoring and comparing motor cars, on bridge-whist and post-mortems, on moving-pictures and potboilers ... They suffer from anemia, from lack of appetite and curiosity for the human scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between structural lack of access and voluntary disengagement; measure audience interest and attention as an independent limiting factor on information uptake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social set determines admissible information and judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: In the social set ... it is finally decided in each phase of a discussion which authorities and which sources of information are admissible, and which not; opinions encounter the canons of Family Tradition, Respectability, Propriety, Dignity, Taste and Form, which make up the social set's picture of itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how group membership conditions what information is trusted or considered relevant. Check whether content aligns with the norms and sanctioned authorities of target social sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of social leaders and inter-set channels
rubrics_metrics.description: The social leaders ... are peculiarly sensitive ... They act as a kind of ministry of foreign affairs ... there come to be established personal channels from one set to another, through which Tarde's laws of imitation operate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify opinion leaders and cross-set connectors; measure their influence as channels for transmitting standards and opinions between social groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Radiant points of conventionality and imitation patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Some sets become 'radiant points of conventionality' — the social superior is likely to be imitated by the social inferior; imitation flows from powerful/successful/rich/urban sets outward, often with international centers like London.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess cultural hegemony and the directionality of influence when judging how news or norms propagate. Consider prestige centers and their symbolic power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal contact versus mediated accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Where personal channels exist there are personal contacts through which a circulation of standards takes place; but for large sections of the population there are no such channels, and the patented accounts of society and the moving pictures of high life have to serve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish direct interpersonal transmission from mediated representations; measure reliance on second-hand portrayals where personal contact is absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time and attention are severely limited
rubrics_metrics.description: Over three quarters of those in the selected groups rate rather low the attention they give to printed news ... most people have a small amount of time each day directly exposed to information from our unseen environment (a quarter of an hour is often cited).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use limited daily attention as a constraint when designing or evaluating news content (length, prominence, frequency). Empirical attention measures (minutes/day, number of papers read) are relevant metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution of reader interest across news features
rubrics_metrics.description: When asked what features interest them most, respondents prioritized general news, editorials, politics, finance, foreign news, local — with about 67.5% picking features dealing with public affairs; preferences vary by group (gender, occupation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare audience preferences to editorial allocation; evaluate alignment or mismatch between content mix and audience interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mismatch between newspaper space allocation and audience preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysis of newspaper subject-matter showed large proportions assigned to news, special features, opinion and advertisements; after excluding ads, about 76.5% of edited space dealt with public-affairs-related items — roughly corresponding to earlier audience preferences but changes over time imply possible mismatch for broader populations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use space allocation as a proxy for editorial priorities and compare with demographic audience data; expect variation over time and across populations (urban vs typical groups).

rubrics_metrics.name: Words are imperfect vehicles for meaning; need for clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Words are transmitted by wire or radio; language is not a perfect vehicle of meanings ... Words, like currency, are turned over and over again, to evoke one set of images to-day, another to-morrow. No certainty that the same word will call out exactly the same idea in the reader's mind as in the reporter's.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize clarity, simplicity, and avoidance of ambiguous terms in news writing and headlines; test for whether words evoke intended images for target audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compression, coding, and condensation reduce nuance
rubrics_metrics.description: Telegraphy is expensive and press service news is usually coded; a long statement may be telescoped so that a few words must stand for a whole succession of acts, thoughts, feelings and consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how condensation (headlines, wires, summaries) strips context and nuance; where possible provide accessible follow-ups or annotations to restore critical detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation, transmission errors and cumulative uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: News may be culled from long speeches in a foreign tongue, translated, coded, and then decoded — the substance is telescoped and meaning can be altered in transmission; 'Words, like money, are tokens of value' with 'war fluctuation on word exchanges.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for translation and retransmission loss when assessing reliability of foreign reporting; consider provenance, eyewitness chain, and intervening actors in credibility judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation in literacy and comprehension among audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Millions of those who are watching him can read hardly at all. Millions more can read the words but cannot understand them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Segment audiences by literacy and comprehension levels when designing news content; use plain language and multimodal supports (images, captions) to reach less literate groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lucidity of mind as criterion for effective thinking about public affairs
rubrics_metrics.description: The power to dissociate superficial analogies, attend to differences and appreciate variety is lucidity of mind ... in truly effective thinking the prime necessity is to liquidate judgments, regain an innocent eye, disentangle feelings, be curious and open-hearted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As an evaluative dimension, measure whether reporting and commentary encourage discriminating thought, highlight distinctions rather than crude analogies, and foster curiosity rather than premature judgement.
